title: Introduction to Derivative-Free Optimization — table of contents (Conn, Scheinberg, Vicente; SIAM MPS-SIAM Series on Optimization 8, 2009)
contribution: The authors' own organisation of DFO (TOC only, typeset 2008/11/17): about 100 pages of sampling, model classes and geometry (Part I) before any optimization framework, then direct search, simplex-gradient line search and trust region (Part II, the 34-page trust-region framework chapter the longest), with constraints, surrogates and global/mixed-integer problems compressed into a short Part III; every named guarantee is global convergence (pp. 1-3).
problem_entry: Title level: Ch. 1 makes the case for DFO and states its limits before any tool: why DFO, examples, limitations of DFO (section 1.3, book p. 5), how DFO algorithms should work (section 1.4, book p. 7) (p. 1).
key_idea: Toolkit first: Part I (book pp. 13-112) is ordered by model class (linear, interpolation, regression, underdetermined) with a reused section skeleton (basic concepts -> Lagrange polynomials -> Lambda-poisedness -> condition number) and ends with a whole chapter on ensuring well poisedness (Ch. 6, incl. fully linear/fully quadratic models, section 6.1); Part II states the trust-region framework and 'conditions on the trust-region models' (sections 10.1-10.2) before the instances 'DFO', Powell's methods and wedge methods (Ch. 11) (pp. 1-3).
assumptions: Title level: smoothness is the default; nonsmoothness only in section 7.4 (direct search); noise only in section 9.3; constraints only in Part III (Ch. 13); no title mentions probability or stochastic models (pp. 1-3).
proof_devices: positive spanning sets and positive bases (section 2.1, p. 1; title only)
Lagrange polynomials and Lambda-poisedness for interpolation, regression and underdetermined models (sections 3.2-3.3, 4.2-4.3, 5.2, pp. 1-2; title only)
condition number as a measure of well poisedness (sections 3.4, 4.4, p. 1; title only)
fully linear and fully quadratic models; pivotal algorithms for well poisedness (sections 6.1, 6.3, p. 2; title only)
integer lattices for simple decrease vs imposed sufficient decrease (sections 7.5, 7.7, p. 2; title only)
model accuracy in larger concentric balls (section 10.7, p. 3; title only)
all named guarantees are global convergence: sections 7.3, 7.4, 8.3, 9.2, 10.4, 10.6; no title contains complexity or rate (pp. 2-3)
experiments: None at title level: no chapter or section on numerical comparison or benchmarking; software only in a 4-page appendix (book pp. 251-254) (p. 3). Reviewer B006 says the introduction holds the only comparison (B006 p. 1).
positioning: Named methods get sections: Nelder-Mead (8.1-8.2), MADS (7.6), implicit filtering (9.4), Powell's methods (11.3) next to the 'DFO' approach (11.2), wedge methods (11.4); direct search (48 pp.) and trust region (54 pp.) get comparable space; surrogates get a chapter (Ch. 12) (pp. 2-3).
writing: Exercises close every chapter except 1, 11 and 13; notes-and-references sections close Ch. 4-11 only; Ch. 3 and Ch. 4 reuse the same four-section skeleton (pp. 1-3).
limits_future: Left out or compressed at title level: complexity/rates, probabilistic or stochastic models, noise beyond section 9.3, one-dimensional methods, problem structure (least squares), ML, constraints (Part III only), global and mixed-integer problems (one section, book pp. 249-250), benchmarking, software beyond an appendix (pp. 1-3). Card includes a reading path through the book for this skill's lens (card writer's suggestion, not the authors').

method_links.note: Stated at the level of the book's organisation (co-authored): geometry organises Part I, a whole chapter (Ch. 6) and eight section titles on poisedness. Dating agrees with C8: titles speak of ensuring well poisedness (2008 maintain-throughout position); the minimal-safeguard stance is not visible at title level.

Weak, title level: trust-region framework kept, the change stated as 'conditions on the trust-region models' (10.2) before DF instances; a globally convergent Nelder-Mead variant (8.3) repairs rather than replaces a trusted method.
Deterministic precursor: fully linear / fully quadratic models (6.1) and model conditions (10.2) are the certified class that BSV 2014 requires only with probability p; no probability in any title.
Dating: all named guarantees are global convergence, no complexity; the first rung of Taste mark 7's progression (complexity arrives with S088, S104).
No section compares methods or estimators numerically; software only as an appendix.
No structure-specific section (least squares, partial separability) at title level.
Constraints, global and mixed-integer problems compressed into Part III, nonsmoothness into one direct-search section (7.4); the book body stays unread, its TOC is now verified.

Title level: Ch. 10 has a section titled 'Conditions on the trust-region models' (10.2); that the chapter is the 1997/2009 shared framework of the Conn lens is an inference from the titles (chapter not read).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Ch. 10 framework with explicit conditions on the models, then Ch. 11 instances (DFO, Powell's methods, wedge methods); title level only

transferable: Toolkit first: collect the analytical machinery (sample-set geometry, model error bounds) in one part and present each algorithm family as a user of it (pp. 1-2)

title: Errata to Introduction to Derivative-Free Optimization (05/17/2015)
contribution: Author-maintained errata for the first printing (18 items): one theorem re-proved with new constants and a stated condition under which the original statement holds (Thm 2.13, linear regression bounds), corrected constants of the quadratic-regression bounds (book p. 69), corrected Lambda values and example sets, and precision fixes; 13 of 18 items fall in Part I, none in the convergence chapters 8-11; four readers credited by name (pp. 1-3).
problem_entry: Public correction of a published textbook six years after publication, item by item (page, line, old text, corrected text) (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Item 3 re-proves Theorem 2.13 for the free-intercept linear regression model: coefficient error = M-dagger times the Taylor residual, scaling identity (2.9) M-dagger = diag(1, (1/Delta)I) M-hat-dagger, kappa_eg = nu(1 + p^{1/2}||M-hat-dagger||/2), kappa_ef = 2 kappa_eg + nu/2; the book's statement holds for the model anchored at f(y0), whose g is the regression simplex gradient of book p. 33 (pp. 1-2).
assumptions: Corrections of stated assumptions/definitions: free intercept vs anchored regression model (items 3-4); a Euclidean ball, not the ball described as squared, in the Lambda examples (item 7); Frobenius norm over the upper or lower triangular part of the Hessian (item 12); finiteness of the positive bases from which poll directions are extracted (item 16) (pp. 1-3).
proof_devices: coefficient error = pseudo-inverse times Taylor residual, |r_i| <= (nu/2)Delta^2, with y0 = 0 without loss of generality (item 3, p. 1)
diagonal scaling (2.9) separating the radius from the geometry of the scaled matrix (item 3, p. 1)
bounds on the whole ball B(y0; Delta): gradient kappa_eg Delta, value kappa_ef Delta^2 (item 3, p. 2)
proof left to the reader reworded: Exercise 10 now asks to show (2.9) first; a claim that a step is obvious replaced by a pointer to arguments already seen (items 5-6, p. 2)
experiments: Not applicable; corrected computed numbers in examples: Lambda values in the captions of Figs 3.1-3.3 (294, 5324, 492624), Lambda on book p. 98 (5324, with a factor-4 scaling sentence removed), example sets Y1, Y2 on book p. 99 (pp. 2-3).
positioning: Acknowledges all readers and names four who reported errors: Griewank, Hare, Le Digabel, Vaz (p. 3).
writing: Each item: book page, usually with the line (negative from below), old text in quotation marks where a sentence changes, corrected version; the theorem correction includes a proof sketch, a footnote on the Moore-Penrose inverse and the validity condition of the old statement (pp. 1-3).
limits_future: Distribution: Ch. 1: 2 items, Part I: 13 (Ch. 2: 4, Ch. 3: 4, Ch. 4: 1, Ch. 5: 1, Ch. 6: 3), Part II: 1 (Ch. 7), Part III: 2; none in Ch. 8-11. The sheet does not say why the Lambda values changed or which corrections came from readers (pp. 1-3).

title: Derivation of Error Bounds for Quadratic Regression (01/27/2011) — addendum to Introduction to Derivative-Free Optimization
contribution: Two-page author note supplying the derivation of the book's Theorem 4.13 (quadratic regression error bounds in terms of the scaled regression matrix): Hessian error O(Delta), gradient O(Delta^2), value O(Delta^3), with constants = nu2 x ||M-dagger|| x explicit dimension factors n^{1/2} and p-bar^{1/2}; B002 item 11 later prints the same constants for book p. 69, with ||Sigma-hat^{-1}|| in place of ||M-dagger|| (pp. 1-2).
problem_entry: A printed theorem (4.13) whose derivation the book omitted; the note gives no reason for publishing separately. Context (inference): S025 (2008) stated Lambda-based regression bounds without proofs as straightforward adaptations [card S025, p. 14]; B002 item 11 corrects book p. 69 to exactly these constants (p. 1).
key_idea: Least-squares coefficients: the coefficient error equals the pseudo-inverse applied to the Taylor residual (0.1); a diagonal scaling (0.2) gives each block (value, gradient, Hessian) its own power of Delta, with the geometry entering only through the scaled pseudo-inverse; one mean-value step moves the bounds from the centre to the ball (pp. 1-2).
assumptions: Lipschitz Hessian (constant nu2 > 0); y0 = 0 without loss of generality (argument at the end of the proof of the book's Theorem 3.16); M full column rank, M-dagger = (M^T M)^{-1} M^T; scaled set in B(0; 1); free-intercept model m(y) = c + g^T y + (1/2) y^T H y (p. 1).
proof_devices: Taylor residual of the second-order Taylor coefficients at the sample points, |r_i| <= (nu/2)Delta^3 (p. 1)
pseudo-inverse identity (0.1): coefficient error = M-dagger r (p. 1)
diagonal scaling (0.2): M-dagger = diag(1, (1/Delta)I_n, (1/Delta^2)I_pbar) M-hat-dagger, pbar = n(n+1)/2 (p. 1)

block bounds: Hessian coefficients O(Delta) with factor pbar^{1/2} nu2/2 ||M-dagger||, sqrt(2) from vec to matrix norm (0.3); gradient at y0 O(Delta^2) with factor n^{1/2} nu2/2 ||M-dagger|| (0.4) (pp. 1-2)

mean-value transfer from the centre to the ball: gradient bound (nu2 + ((n^{1/2} + sqrt(2) pbar^{1/2})/2) nu2 ||M-dagger||) Delta^2, value bound (nu2/2 + (1/2 + n^{1/2}/2 + sqrt(2) pbar^{1/2}/4) nu2 ||M-dagger||) Delta^3 (p. 2)

reading note (not a finding): nu printed where nu2 is assumed; ||M-dagger|| printed where the scaled M-hat-dagger appears meant; the step to the factors pbar^{1/2}, n^{1/2} is not written out and was not checked (pp. 1-2)
positioning: No citations; refers only to the book's Theorems 3.16 and 4.13 and equation (3.1) (pp. 1-2).
writing: One sentence of motivation, then numbered equations (0.1)-(0.4); the footnote on the Moore-Penrose inverse is word for word the one in B002 item 3 (p. 1; B002 p. 1).
limits_future: Deterministic, smooth (Lipschitz Hessian), full-column-rank M; noise not treated although regression is the group's proposed tool for noisy data [card S025, p. 1] (pp. 1-2).

method_links.note: Method 4 step 2 (model error <= poisedness constant x radius) in regression form, with the constant written out as nu2 x ||M-hat-dagger|| x dimension factors.

Weak: n and pbar = n(n+1)/2 dependence explicit in every constant; S088 later tracks n the same way and improves the book's Lambda-poisedness gradient bound [card S088, pp. 9-11].

title: Review of Introduction to Derivative-Free Optimization (Mathematics of Computation 79(271), 2010)
contribution: External review by J. L. Nazareth (University of Washington; reviewer's voice, not the authors'): a state-of-the-art, gracefully written, well-organised monograph whose Part I toolkit (poisedness the key notion) serves Part II, with derivative-free trust-region methods the centerpiece; criticised for theory-only exercises, atypical examples, few numerics, no implementation detail (not algorithmic engineering), no one-dimensional theory, and no adequate treatment of the DFO / non-differentiable intersection (pp. 1-3).
problem_entry: Reviewer's framing: benign problems (smooth, unconstrained, up to about a hundred variables) made hard by missing derivatives and expensive or noisy evaluations; DFO separated from non-differentiable optimization because its convergence relies on smoothness (p. 1). Second-hand (reviewer quoting the preface, book pp. xi-xii): the aim is theory to the extent needed to understand what ensures convergence and how it affects algorithm design (p. 1).
key_idea: Reviewer's reading: Part I is the mathematical toolkit (positive spanning sets, poisedness, Lambda-poisedness, condition numbers, three model-class chapters, set improvement); Part II uses it; two trust-region frameworks with first- and second-order global convergence underlie DFO, Powell's and wedge methods (p. 2).
assumptions: Reviewer: the class is reasonably smooth, unconstrained, relatively small n (p. 1).
experiments: Reviewer: few numerical illustrations (compared with Kelley), no implementational details (p. 3).
positioning: Reviewer places the book in his own framework of algorithmic science and engineering (its theoretical algorithmic science mode), citing his own SIAM News article; useful to practitioners, researchers and software developers (p. 3).
writing: Reviewer: gracefully written, well organised, timely; Part I nicely organised and well presented (pp. 2-3).
limits_future: Reviewer's criticisms: exercises mostly elaborations of theory (reduces use for an introductory course); introductory examples atypical; few numerics; unidimensional (Brent) theory not covered; DFO / non-differentiable intersection not adequately addressed (pp. 2-3).

method_links.note: Peer view: poisedness is the key notion; comprehensive treatment of interpolation-set quality.
Peer view, weak: trust-region frameworks with global convergence proofs are the basis of several practical algorithms.
Agrees with C1: a theory monograph with few numerics and no implementation detail, like the pure-analysis papers.
Peer view: not on the algorithmic-engineering side (Quote 2); theoretical algorithmic science mode.
Peer view: smooth, unconstrained, small-n class; DFO / nonsmooth intersection not adequately addressed.
Peer view: few numerical comparisons.

transferable: Avoid the two criticisms both reviews share: exercises that only extend the theory, and too few worked numerical examples (pp. 2-3; B006 p. 2)
Separate your problem class from its neighbour explicitly and name the assumption that separates them (derivative-free vs non-differentiable; smoothness) (p. 1)
coauthors: none (external review by J. L. Nazareth, University of Washington; not a Scheinberg work)

quotes.text: The important intersection between derivative-free optimization and non-differentiable optimization is not adequately addressed.
its focus is not on the “algorithmic engineering” side of the subject.

title: Review of Introduction to Derivative-Free Optimization (SIAM Review 53(2), 2011, book reviews)
contribution: External review by Dominique Orban (Ecole Polytechnique de Montreal; reviewer's voice, not the authors'): the de facto authoritative DFO text, teaching direct-search and model-based methods with their limitations, Part I/Part II split usable as a course order, clearly stated similarities and differences with classical trust region; shortcomings: the introduction holds the only comparison between methods (comparison reported as not an objective), exercises extend theory, few examples, research-grade software (pp. 1-2). Year corrected from 2010 (batch plan) to 2011: SIAM Review 53(2), 2011, pp. 395-396 per the authors' book page; Crossref lists the 53(2) Book Reviews section as pp. 375-405.
problem_entry: Reviewer: the authoritative text for optimization without available derivatives; favourite application in the introduction: tuning algorithmic parameters, a nonsmooth noisy problem (p. 1).
key_idea: Reviewer's reading: technical background (Part I) and algorithms (Part II) separated so a reader can start algorithm design after a cursory Part I; positive spanning sets and poisedness make Nelder-Mead a didactic illustration of the direct-search framework; line search is a line-search variant of the trust-region methods with simplex gradients (pp. 1-2).
assumptions: Reviewer: Lipschitz-continuous gradient or Hessian and models on a well-poised sample set, unlike the nonsmooth (locally Lipschitz) chapters of Conn-Gould-Toint's Trust-Region Methods (p. 2).
experiments: Reviewer: the introduction gives the only comparison between methods in the book; he reports the authors saying comparison is intricate and not an objective (p. 1).
positioning: Reviewer: trust-region chapters read against Conn-Gould-Toint (one shared author); surrogates likened to a fortune teller, included in Part II methods while keeping convergence; all three authors central players; essential as text and reference (p. 2).
writing: Reviewer: clarity, consistency and rigor of Part I; useful end-of-chapter notes and extensive bibliography (p. 2).
limits_future: Reviewer: exercises mostly extensions of theory; few examples; wishes for bare-bones implementations in Part II exercises; listed software research grade, not accessible to non-experts (p. 2).

method_links.note: Peer view: similarities and differences with classical trust region clearly stated (keep the classical method, say what changes).
Peer view: poisedness and positive spanning sets described with clarity, consistency and rigor.
Peer-reported 2009 position: the only comparison is in the introduction and comparison was not an objective; dates the head-to-head habit to after the book [cards S023, S006].
Agrees with C1: few examples, no bare-bones implementations.
Peer view: Lipschitz gradient/Hessian assumed; nonsmooth trust-region theory lives elsewhere; research-grade software (blind spot: production-grade software).
Peer view: the trust-region chapters stand next to Conn-Gould-Toint's Trust-Region Methods, one author in common.

transferable: When a method is a variant of a classical one, state the similarities and the differences explicitly (p. 2)
Give each algorithm a bare-bones implementation or exercise so readers see its behaviour, not only its theory (p. 2)
coauthors: none (external review by Dominique Orban, Ecole Polytechnique de Montreal; not a Scheinberg work)
